newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan to contact CEPA to terminate power deal.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan to contact CEPA to terminate power deal.

text.p: The Pakistan government said on Wednesday it would contact the Hong Kong-based Consolidated Electric Power of Asia Ltd (CEPA) for the termination of a deal for CEPA to set up a $5.5 billion power plant.

Water and Power Minister Nisar Ali Khan told Reuters that the government had decided in principle to terminate the deal because of a very high production cost of power from the planned project at Keti Bunder in the southern province of Sindh.
But he said the government wanted termination by mutual agreement. "We are contacting CEPA people for mutual agreement."

Earlier on Wednesday, opposition leader Benazir Bhutto threatened to go to court to defend the CEPA project, saying that the government move to terminate the deal was discriminatory against Sindh, her home province.
"We will strongly protest,...this is criminal," the former prime minister said while speaking on the issue in the National Assembly (lower house of parliament).
"We will consult our legal experts to go to the Supreme Court to see if it was discrimination against a smaller province," she said.
Her remarks followed a statement by Khan in the Assembly on Tuesday that Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government had decided to terminate the deal with CEPA by "mutual agreement".

A CEPA official in Islamabad said the government had not conveyed its decision to his company, in which U.S. power giant Southern Co has an 80 percent and Hong Kong's Hopewell Holdings Ltd 20 percent.
"We have absolutely no official information or intimation of termination of the contract," CEPA resident director Latif Chaudhry told Reuters by telephone.
"As far as we are concerned, we are working as usual, all our staff here, in Karachi and in Hong Kong are working as they have always been working," Chaudhry said.

Earlier this month, a Pakistan government official had said that the Econonomic Coordination Committee of the cabinet had decided to re-negotiate the deal with CEPA, which was struck in June 1995 when Islamabad issued a Letter of Support, enabling the power company to complete other formalities.
Under the agreement, CEPA was to build eight 660-megwatt coal-based thermal power plants at Keti Bundar, about 60 km (37 miles) west of the port city of Karachi.
CEPA also had plans to develop a 14-meter deep sea port in Sindh and also set up a special industrial zone at the site with a total cost of $1.0 billion.
"We are still committed to the terms of MOU (memorandum of understanding) for setting up the port," Khan said.
Khan denied that the government was reveiwing the deals signed by the previous government with a number of international companies for setting up thermal power stations.
He said the government had only set up a committee to find ways how to make tariffs of these plants less expensive.
